title: Tactics and traps of the Dragon: Bh6, Nd5, the h-file, the c-file and the exchange sacrifice
outcomes: Judges whether the bishop trade on h6 is safe by counting the guards of the knight on d4 (the bishop on e3 and the queen on d2) and shows the refutation when it is not
Finds White's h-file sequence (queen takes h7 with check, then the bishop to h6) and Black's counter-sacrifice when the attack is a move too slow
Counts attackers and guards on c3 and chooses between the knight jump to d5, the exchange sacrifice and a quiet move

Names the common case of the exchange sacrifice on c3 (bishop on g7, a queenside king, a queen ready for a5) and the general principle behind it (a target the pawn recapture exposes), and recognises edits that make it fail
Explains in his or her own words why each of six shapes works, when it fails, and what a beginner could set up on a board

steps.text: **Six shapes decide most Dragon games.** The bishop trade on h6. The h-file. The knight jump to d5. The exchange sacrifice on c3. Queen-and-rook pressure on the c-file. King hunts near the back rank. By the end you can look at a position you have never seen and say which shape is in the air and what it needs. You are learning conditions, not lines. Each shape is shown working and failing.

**The trade on h6.** Black's bishop on g7 guards the dark squares around the king. A white bishop on h6 attacks it. If Black trades, White's queen lands on h6; if Black retreats to h8, the queen gets the h-file. Either way a defender is gone. The price: the bishop on e3 and the queen on d2 are the two guards of the knight on d4, and this plan spends both. Three boards follow, each with a different answer.

steps.prompt: The three positions gave three different answers to the same bishop move. Before reading on, write what separates them: look at the h-pawns and at where Black's queen stands.

steps.text: **What separates the three.** [I] In the first two, a black pawn on h5 faces White's pawn on h4, so the h-file stays closed and the trade only removes a defender. In the third White has no h-pawn, the file is open for the rook on h1, and Black's queen is far away: the queen lands on h2 and Bg5 attacks the knight on f6, a guard of h7. Scores are [V]; this explanation is inference.

steps.caption: Why the trade fails here. The bishop on e3 and the queen on d2 both guard the knight on d4. Bh6 spends the bishop, the recapture on h6 spends the queen, so the knight on c6 simply takes a loose knight. The engine puts White about five pawns down (depth 16). Before any bishop trade, count the guards of d4. The hook answered: the first position is the mistake.

steps.text: **Conditions, not a rule.** The trade tends to work when the h-file is open or opening and when taking on h6 is worse for Black than declining. It fails when the bishop and the queen are the only guards of a loose knight, here on d4. [I] The queen leaving d2 also loosens c2, but d4 decides this position. [H] Many amateur Dragon games are lost by playing the trade because it looks aggressive, without counting the guards. Test this on your own games.

**The h-file.** White pushes the h-pawn to h5 to trade it for the pawn on g6, the shield of Black's king. When the file opens, a rook stands behind and the other pieces join: the bishop removes the g7 defender, the queen lands on h6 or h4. Capablanca noted that sacrifices on a castled king work through coordination [S]; I apply that to h-file attacks [I]: cover stripped, then queen, rook and a minor piece finish.

steps.text: **Count the race.** Edward Lasker noted that when kings castle on opposite wings pawns are cheap and speed decides [S]; our notes pair Philidor with him [S]. So count: how many moves does each side need to open a line against the enemy king, and who can slow the other with one forcing move? [I] This counting is a heuristic, not a law. One worked count follows, then three positions to judge before you read the engine's verdict.

steps.caption: Worked count (the Navara-Hou Yifan position again). White: h5, hxg6, then the queen to h4 puts queen and rook on the file, three moves. Black: a rook to c8 and a knight move open the c-file, about two moves [I]. The gap is one move, and the pawn trade on g6 is the forcing move that gains White the time. [I] Heuristic only.

steps.text: **The jump to d5.** When Black chases the knight with ...b5-b4, the knight often has a good square on d5. If Black takes with the bishop, the e-pawn recaptures and Black's bishop on e6 is gone; if Black takes with the knight, a bishop recaptures. The jump works when d5 is reachable, when White can recapture, and when the trade does not remove a guard of a key square.

steps.text: **The exchange sacrifice on c3.** Black gives a rook for the knight. In the common case a pawn recaptures, White's king (usually on the queenside) has lost its cover, the queen reaches a5, and the bishop on g7 stands behind the knight on f6. [I] The general principle: the rook is paid for by a target the pawn recapture exposes: a king without cover, a loose pawn, a long diagonal. Nimzowitsch argued for giving material to open a line, but only after quieter attacks have been tried [S].

steps.text: **Queen and rook on the c-file.** Black's queen on a5 and rook on c8 aim at the knight on c3 and the king behind it. Count who guards what: the pawn on b2 and the queen on d2 guard c3, the black queen attacks it, and the rook waits behind its own knight. [H] A single missed guard, usually of the knight on c3 or the pawn on c2, is behind many Dragon blunders. The habit to train is: who guards what.

steps.caption: Who guards what? The knight on c3 has two defenders (the pawn on b2 and the queen on d2) and one attacker (the queen on a5). The rook on c8 is blocked by its own knight, but a single knight move opens the file.

steps.text: **Traps: what actually occurs.** In a local file of well over a thousand high-level Dragon games (both players 2400+, 2012 to 2026, online rapid and blitz included; see the sources for the filter) [V], the three mistakes on these boards, three specific positions, never occur: players avoid them. They are errors a lower-rated player might make, and the engine shows that each loses. [I] You learn the shape, not the line. The move 7...Ng4 below does occur, in 3 games, and is good.

steps.text: **What the six shapes share.** Each removes or overloads a guard: the bishop on g7, the pawn on g6, the guards of d4, the knight on c3. Before a forcing move ask who guards what and what leaves. Edward Lasker's rule applies too: every pawn move leaves something behind [S]. Nimzowitsch spoke of giving material to clear the way [S]; Petrosian used the positional exchange sacrifice [S], a different purpose from a quick attack [I].

steps.prompt: [H] Hypothesis: the six shapes can be reduced to one question, "who guards what, and what leaves?". Do you agree? Name a Dragon shape (or a position from your own games) that this question would not catch.

Teach it back. Imagine a beginner who has just seen the Dragon. In your own words write: which of the six shapes you would teach first, when it works, one example a beginner can set up on a board, and one warning.

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did you say when the trade on h6 works and when it fails? Did you give an example a beginner could set up on a board? Did you name the common case of the exchange sacrifice (bishop on g7, king on the queenside, a queen ready to arrive) and the general principle (a target the recapture exposes)? Did you name one mistake, such as spending both guards of the knight on d4? The app grades nothing. Compare with a friend or coach.

**Recap.**
- The trade on h6 works when the h-file is ready; it fails when the bishop and queen are the only guards of a loose knight on d4.
- The h-file attack is a team job and a race.
- Count attackers and guards before the jump to d5.
- The exchange sacrifice needs a target the recapture exposes: often a queenside king, sometimes a loose pawn.
- Queen and rook on the c-file make c3 the square to count.
- Ask who guards what before every forcing move.

The file was counted as 1,375 games in an earlier run; a later recount with a broader filter found 1,571 with the Dragon move order, so the exact total is approximate and the filter should be re-run before the number is quoted again. Games used: Horvath-Kantor 2018, Iordachescu-Jianu 2013, Paravyan-Golubev 2022, Navara-Hou Yifan 2013 (blitz), Garcia Pantoja-Golubev 2022, Vasquez Schroeder-Golubev 2022, Erigaisi-Mamedov 2024, Godart-Dgebuadze 2020, Ter Sahakyan-Nakamura 2026, Matinian-Kanter 2013.
